title: Pointer Arithmetic and Array Decay
quickIdea: Pointer arithmetic is scaled by the size of the pointed-to type, and a[i] is defined as *(a + i) - so the index form and the pointer form are the same expression, and p2 - p1 counts elements, not bytes.
remember: p + k advances k * sizeof(*p) bytes. On an int * with 4-byte ints, p + 1 adds 4; on a char * it adds 1.
a[i] means *(a + i), so a[i] and i[a] are the same object; that is why 2[p] is legal C and equals p[2].

An array name decays to &a[0] in every expression except three: as the operand of sizeof, as the operand of unary &, and as a string-literal initialiser. sizeof(a) is the whole array, sizeof(p) is the pointer.
&a and a hold the same address but have different types: a + 1 moves one element while &a + 1 moves past the whole array.
p2 - p1 has type ptrdiff_t and counts elements. Subtracting or comparing pointers is defined only within one array, or one past its end.
An array name is not assignable: a++ and a = p do not compile, while p++ on a pointer variable does.
A 2-D parameter int arr[][C] is adjusted to int (*arr)[C]; only the first dimension may be omitted.

example.work: p points at a[0] and q at a[1]. q - p counts elements between two double pointers, so it is 1 even though the addresses differ by 8 bytes. *q - *p subtracts the stored values, 25.0 - 20.0 = 5.0, and the cast to int gives 5.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2024 Set 2 Q.26 prints 1,5, and its distractors 8,5 and 1,8 are exactly the two mistakes: counting bytes instead of elements, and forgetting that the second value is a subtraction of the stored numbers. GATE CSE 2017 Set 2 Q.55 hides the same identity behind 2[p] - 6[p].

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: int a[6] = {10,20,30,40,50,60}; int *p = a + 2; what are *(p + 3) - *p and p - a?
variations.answer: 30 and 2: *(p + 3) is a[5] = 60 and *p is a[2] = 30, so the difference is 30, and p - a counts elements and gives 2 rather than the 8 bytes.
variations.why: The same two rules as the 2024 question with a base offset, which is where students start adding bytes by hand.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why is a[i] the same object as i[a]?
variations.answer: Because both expand to *(a + i), and the addition of an integer and a pointer is commutative in C. The subscript operator is defined that way, not as a special array operation.
variations.why: Turns a curiosity into the definition it comes from, which is what the 2017 question relies on.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: With p == c and c holding "GATECSIT2017", what does c + 2[p] - 6[p] - 1 point at?
variations.answer: c + 10, because 2[p] is 'T' (84) and 6[p] is 'I' (73), so the offset is 84 - 73 - 1 = 10; strlen from there counts the two characters '1' and '7'.
variations.why: The 2017 question's reasoning step, restated as a pointer question instead of a strlen question.

trap.what: Reading p - q as a byte distance.
trap.why: Subtraction of two pointers of the same type is defined in elements. The compiler divides the address difference by sizeof(*p) for you, so on doubles an adjacent pair differs by 1 while the addresses differ by 8.
trap.counterexample: With double a[2] at address 1000, &a[1] - &a[0] is 1, although (char *)&a[1] - (char *)&a[0] is 8.

check.question: int a[10]; with 4-byte ints and 8-byte pointers, what do sizeof a and sizeof(a + 0) give?
check.explanation: sizeof a sees the array itself, one of the three no-decay contexts, and gives 10 x 4. a + 0 is already a pointer expression, so sizeof sees a pointer.
